title: For Loops (Walking Through Things)
story: You're the teacher taking attendance. You have a list of names and you call each one: 'Is Alex here? Is Jordan here? Is Sam here?' You're walking through the list one name at a time — and that's exactly what a `for` loop does.
why: Real programs deal with lists of things all the time — friend names, game scores, shopping items, photo albums. `for` loops let you walk through each item in a list and do something with it, without writing the same code over and over.
analogy: A for-loop is like a librarian checking each book on a shelf — they pick up one book at a time, look at it, put it back, and move to the next one, until they've checked them all.
expected_output:
Greeting my friends:
Hi, Maya!
Hi, Leo!
Hi, Priya!
Hi, Kai!
Everyone has been greeted!
try_it: Add your own friends' names to the list and greet them all. Then make a list of your favorite foods and use a for loop to print each one. Try a list of numbers too — can you print each number multiplied by 2 inside the loop?
tips: The variable in `for item in list` is created automatically — no `let` or `var` needed. It gets a new value each time through the loop.
Pick descriptive names for your loop variable: `for friend in friends`, not `for f in friends`.
Lists use square brackets with commas: `["a", "b", "c"]`. The last item doesn't need a trailing comma.
You can put `if`/`else` inside a `for` loop — for example, only greet friends whose names start with a certain letter.
common_mistakes: Writing `for name = in names` instead of `for name in names` — no equals sign, just `in`.
Using `let` before the loop variable: `for let name in names` — the loop creates the variable for you.
Trying to use a `for` loop with just a number range: `for i in 1..5` doesn't work in XIOM — use a `while` loop with a counter instead.
Forgetting the `in` keyword: `for name names {` is missing the `in` — it should be `for name in names {`.
